name: Upland Cress
variety: Upland cress crop type; cultivar unspecified
summary: A cool-season leafy biennial grown for peppery greens. Kentucky State University Extension gives a documented germination range; cultivar and seed-lot behavior are not specified.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Barbarea verna in Brassicaceae and describes it as a biennial temperate species used for food. KSU Extension identifies upland cress as a leafy green; no cultivar is named here.

cultivation.short: Keep the leafy crop cool and evenly moist
cultivation.guidance: KSU Extension describes upland cress as a peppery leafy green and gives rich, moist, well-drained soil as growing context. This is garden-soil evidence; no hydroponic recipe or indoor-light equivalence is established.

growth.guidance: Kew classifies the accepted species as biennial. No named cultivar, mature dimensions or reliable container-size target is established by the selected sources.

harvest.short: Harvest leaves as a peppery green
harvest.guidance: KSU Extension presents upland cress as an edible leafy green. A cultivar-specific harvest age, regrowth interval or harvest method is not established in the selected evidence.

problems.short: Avoid letting the seedbed dry during establishment
problems.guidance: KSU Extension describes a preference for moist, well-drained conditions. Disease resistance and a crop-specific pest-management schedule remain unestablished.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected KSU guidance is for garden growing and does not validate hydroponic production.

name: Jute Mallow
summary: A warm-season leafy crop also known as molokhia. The University of Minnesota Plant Breeding Center discusses two Corchorus species together, so crop-group guidance is not treated as a cultivar-specific claim.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Corchorus olitorius in Malvaceae. The University of Minnesota source covers both C. olitorius and C. capsularis as jute mallow; this identity represents C. olitorius only, not both species as synonyms.

cultivation.short: Warm-season leafy crop; soil guidance only
cultivation.guidance: The University of Minnesota Plant Breeding Center describes full sun, fertile well-drained soil and indoor starting about six weeks before last frost in its jute-mallow crop guidance. Regional timing is not generalized to other climates or hydroponics.

growth.short: Annual leafy herb grown for foliage
growth.guidance: Kew describes Corchorus olitorius as an annual. The Minnesota source identifies it as a leafy vegetable and fiber crop but also covers C. capsularis; dimensions and cultivar traits are not assigned to this record.

harvest.short: Leaves can be harvested in repeated cuts
harvest.guidance: The University of Minnesota source describes bunch or leaf harvest starting around 40 days and then every two to three weeks through summer for its jute-mallow guidance. The timing is crop-level regional guidance, not a cultivar guarantee.

problems.short: Small seed can make uniform establishment difficult
problems.guidance: The University of Minnesota source notes that small seeds can make consistent germination difficult and suggests seed tape or starting indoors and transplanting. No disease resistance or specific pest claim is made.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source addresses soil growing and does not establish hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: A controlled growth habit for indoor system compatibility is not established.

height.reason: The source covers two species and does not establish a cultivar-specific height for this identity.

spread.reason: No relevant indoor mature spread is supported.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not converted to hydroponic pod spacing.

light.reason: Full sun is an outdoor exposure statement, not an indoor grow-light classification.

name: Bottle Gourd
summary: A vigorous climbing annual grown as a vegetable when young or for mature hard-shelled gourds. The sources describe a large outdoor vine; compact or hydroponic use is not inferred.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Lagenaria siceraria in Cucurbitaceae and describes it as a climbing annual. Bottle, calabash and birdhouse are horticultural/product forms within the species; no named cultivar is established here.

cultivation.short: Needs a warm, sunny site and substantial vine space
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension recommends direct seeding after frost danger has passed and soil reaches about 70°F, in full sun with consistent moisture. Its spacing and soil advice are outdoor crop guidance, not indoor pod spacing.

growth.short: Vigorous climbing annual with long vines
growth.guidance: Kew describes a climbing annual and UNH Extension reports birdhouse-gourd vines can reach 15–35 feet. The vine measurement is for the birdhouse-gourd context and is not presented as a universal cultivar dimension.

harvest.short: Use young fruit as a vegetable or cure mature gourds
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension describes young fruits as edible and mature fruits as hard-shelled ornamental or useful gourds. Do not eat fruit that tastes unusually bitter; the source warns cucurbitacins may be toxic at high concentrations.

problems.short: Cold soil delays establishment; vines require space
problems.guidance: UNH Extension advises waiting until frost danger passes and soil is at least 70°F before sowing and describes a very large vine. No resistance claim or small-space compatibility is made.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected sources document outdoor soil cultivation, not hydroponic production.

growthHabits.reason: A vigorous climbing vine is documented, but the controlled vocabulary does not establish machine-system fit.

height.reason: Vine length is not equivalent to vertical plant height.

spread.reason: Long vine growth is not a finite mature spread value for a container or system.
